extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and attorneys facing PTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing disciplinary proceedings against attorneys registered to practice before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, including evidentiary, procedural, and sanctioning principles applied by the Administrative Law Judge and Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof in PTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: In a disciplinary proceeding, the Director shall have the burden of proving his or her case by clear and convincing evidence (10 C.F.R. § 10.149).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'intermediate standard of clear and convincing evidence' lies between a preponderance of the evidence and proof beyond a reasonable doubt. It has been defined as evidence which produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction as to the truth of the allegations sought to be established (citing Addington v. Texas and Cruzan v. Missouri Dep't of Health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of attorney discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of attorney discipline is to maintain the integrity of the profession, protect the public and the courts, and deter other attorneys from engaging in similar misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline should preserve public confidence in the integrity and trustworthiness of lawyers; protection of the public and bar, not punishment, is the primary purpose. Relevant mitigating and aggravating circumstances must be considered (citing cases such as In re Reback, Coombs v. State Bar of California, In re Slattery). These principles guide assessment under 37 C.F.R. § 10.154(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for assessing sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 10.154(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions are determined by weighing factors identified in 37 C.F.R. § 10.154(b), including public interest, integrity of the profession, protection of the public, deterrence, and relevant mitigating and aggravating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply case-by-case analysis. Consider seriousness of violation, intent, degree of deceit, harm or prejudice caused, prior misconduct (including prior findings such as inequitable conduct), remorse, practitioner's reputation and experience, and whether the misconduct affected tribunal decision-making or client interests. Letters and character evidence must be authenticated to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on fabrication or use of manufactured evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation and use of manufactured evidence (documents altered or created to appear authentic) without timely disclosure is misconduct and 'detracts from the just, speedy and inexpensive determination' of proceedings (Board findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using manufactured evidence without identifying it as such is 'truly extraordinary' and undermines the Board's ability to control proceedings and may tempt semantic games to mislead witnesses and opposing counsel. Prior authorization from the Board should be obtained before using such tactics; failure to do so can lead to sanctions. The extent of sanction depends on intent, harm, and whether the fabricated item was introduced as substantive evidence or used as a demonstrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the Patent Office and related disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must be candid with the Patent Office and opposing parties; violations of 37 C.F.R. Part 10 (e.g., § 10.23(b)(4)-(6), § 10.85(a)(4),(a)(6), § 10.89(c)(1)) are alleged where a practitioner fabricates evidence, misrepresents facts, or fails to disclose material information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentations to the OED or tribunal, and failures to disclose the true nature of exhibits or materials when required, can constitute grounds for suspension or other discipline. Even broad, voluntary statements (e.g., 'fitness to practice has never been called into question') may be scrutinized if factually inaccurate in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference discovery and deposition exhibit rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 41.150-41.158)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference proceedings have limited discovery and specific rules: automatic discovery obligations (service within 21 days of request), restricted additional discovery (authorization by APJ), and strict deposition/exhibit procedures (notice of exhibits, numbering and service of exhibits, filing original transcripts as exhibits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence not taken, sought, or filed in accordance with the Interference Rules is not admissible. For depositions: include list of exhibits in the notice; exhibits relied upon must be numbered and served at that time; objections must be made during the deposition and evidence to cure the objection must be provided during the deposition (unless parties stipulate otherwise); after filing the transcript, a motion to exclude is required to preserve objections. Because cross-examinations occur outside the presiding officer's supervising presence, the parties' conduct is tightly prescribed and the Board may impose sanctions for misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation regarding demonstrative exhibits used in depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a demonstrative exhibit is used (e.g., created to test a witness reaction), the practitioner should not present it in a manner that implies authenticity and must disclose its nature in a timely fashion if it will be relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a demonstrative 'with the feel of authenticity' (adding Bates numbers, cover sheets) without informing opposing counsel or the Board can mislead and prolong issues; if a party intends to rely on testimony elicited from a demonstrative, it should identify the exhibit accordingly (failure to do so risks sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing fabrication vs demonstrative use (intent and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an altered/created document was fabricated to introduce into evidence on substantive issues or was a demonstrative used to develop cross-examination; the practitioner's intent and whether any tribunal reliance occurred are key to sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record shows the item was intended solely as a demonstrative to expose bias and not to be used substantively, and no reliance on it occurred, that mitigates severity. Conversely, fabrication intended for substantive introduction or causing reliance supports more severe sanctions. Evaluate bad faith, evasiveness in explanations, and prolongation of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and consideration of post-hearing mitigation evidence (allocution/affidavit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-hearing affidavits offered for mitigation are within the tribunal's discretion; there is no automatic right to allocution in PTO disciplinary proceedings and Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'ritual of allocution' (personal colloquy) is not guaranteed; documents submitted after hearing adjournment typically require a motion to reopen and must meet motion requirements. Even if considered, an affidavit is not the same as a personal allocution and may not affect sanctions if the matters are already in the record or do not bear on liability or mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication/foundation requirements for mitigation letters and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and other documents submitted in mitigation must be properly authenticated and founded to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proffered letters lack foundation and authentication, they are inadmissible and need not be considered in assessing sanction. Expert testimony and admissible evidence are preferred for matters addressing propriety of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative sanctioning principles and precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should be proportionate and informed by prior disciplinary decisions: similar misconduct has yielded a range of sanctions (private reprimand up to multi-year suspension or disbarment), depending on nature and extent of dishonesty, persistence, harm, and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: forgery and ongoing dishonest acts have led to three-year suspensions; altering documents that did not affect tribunal decision have led to shorter suspensions (e.g., 30 days to 6 months). Mitigating facts (no personal gain, minimal harm, isolated incident) may reduce sanction; prior related misconduct weighs aggravatingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to preserve and raise deposition objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to deposition evidence must be made during the deposition; to preserve them after filing the transcript, a motion to exclude must be filed (37 C.F.R. § 41.155).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely object or preserve objections by motion may forfeit the objection and can affect admissibility and later review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference evidentiary composition and admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference cases are decided primarily on a written record; evidence consists of affidavits, transcripts of depositions, documents and things, and direct testimony is submitted by affidavit with cross-examination via deposition (37 C.F.R. § 41.154(a),(c),(e),(157)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence not taken, sought, or filed in accordance with the Interference Rules is not admissible. The special nature of interference practice (limited discovery, written-record focus) makes adherence to procedural rules critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure from Initial Decision (37 C.F.R. § 10.155)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from the Initial Decision must be filed in duplicate with the Director, Office of Enrollment and Discipline, within 30 days of the Decision and must include exceptions to the Administrative Law Judge's Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file the appeal in accordance with § 10.155 will be deemed acceptance of the Initial Decision and waiver of further administrative and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability and interference substantive context relevant to proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference proceedings determine questions of priority of invention and may determine patentability; patents grant exclusive rights and U.S. law historically applied 'first to invent' standards (35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a)-(f), 135).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the substantive stakes (priority, patentability, monetary significance) explains why fabrication or misleading conduct in interference contexts can have serious consequences. Interference rules and MPEP guidance govern procedure and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning emphasis on deterrence and public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should deter future misconduct by the respondent and others and preserve public confidence that the PTO enforces high ethical standards among registered practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where individual wrongdoing is not severe, a meaningful sanction may be required to signal seriousness to the profession (e.g., a short suspension when conduct stretches limits of trustworthiness). The practitioner's position in the bar and community standing do not necessarily justify reduced sanctions.
